name: Jamal Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Jamal. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that isn't tied to any company, union, party or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at The Anchor, a seafood restaurant on the harbour wall, and I've been there since I was 19, when Mr Okafor (the owner) took me on as an apprentice. I do the fish section: filleting the morning's catch, the grill, the fryer for the fish and chips at lunch. We do two services, and in summer there's a queue out the door by noon.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I learned it all from one man, the old way, standing next to him with a knife. The hard bit is summer, sixteen days straight sometimes, and my fiancée Hana gets fed up. We're getting married next spring, and I've got my own little flat that I bought with help from my dad, so I'm better set than most cooks my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how it should be, if you ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it, and I'd say it to anyone. At the Anchor we'd have a laugh about it over staff dinner. I don't do online, apart from the church group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, and I'm glad. Nobody's going to fillet a sea bass with a computer. I'll keep doing what Mr Okafor taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always: fish section, two services, save what I can for the wedding. I'd keep paying extra off the flat each month. I wouldn't touch any of the AI things, I don't even use the app for the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like a normal Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mr Okafor is in his sixties. What happens to The Anchor in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Okafor's son, Daniel, would probably take over in a few years. Daniel likes gadgets, so maybe a new till. But the kitchen would stay the way his father built it, I'd hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Hana are getting married. Is there anything about money that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The wedding costs a lot, but we've saved for it, and the flat is nearly half paid. A good cook with a trade can always find work around here, there are kitchens all along the front.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the AI hype, to anyone.
I'd joke about it over **staff dinner** at The Anchor.
think: Nobody's going to **fillet a sea bass** with a computer.
I'll keep doing what **Mr Okafor** taught me, the old way.
do: Keep the **fish section** and two services, and save steadily for the **wedding**.
Keep paying **extra off the flat** each month and stay away from AI apps.
feel: **Calm** and settled, like a normal Sunday.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to fillet a sea bass with a computer.
fieldNote: Jamal's identity rests on an **apprenticeship** and loyalty to one owner.
He feels **financially secure**: savings, a part-paid flat and plenty of local kitchens.
He avoids technology entirely, even **banking apps**.

steps.text: Keep the fish section and two services at The Anchor
Pay extra off the flat each month alongside wedding savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one's not about me so much. That one's about Hana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say businesses have the right to run themselves how they want, that's the market. I'd also say people need to work, not wait for handouts. Mostly I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my fish section is fine, but my fiancée Hana answers customers at a bank call centre. That's on the card, plain as day. If her team shrinks, our wedding and our plans for kids all lean on my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and take every extra shift Mr Okafor offers. I'd tell Hana to look now for something more hands-on, maybe at her mum's bakery. And we'd keep the wedding smaller, maybe 80 guests instead of 150.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. For her, for us. Not for my knife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this one is about Hana. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's been at that call centre five years, and she's good with people. But they already brought in a chatbot that answers the easy calls. Her manager told them last month there'd be no new hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Hana's hours went down, what changes at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd live on my pay and her savings for a while. Kids might wait a year or two. I don't want Hana going to the government for help; her family and mine would step in first, that's how we do it.

say: I'd say businesses have the **right** to run how they want.
I'd say people need **to work**, not wait for **handouts**.
think: My **fish section** is fine, but Hana's **call centre** job is on the card.
Our **wedding and kids** would lean on my wage.
do: Take **every extra shift** Mr Okafor offers, especially in the summer rush.
Cut the wedding to **80 guests** instead of 150, and push Hana toward hands-on work.
feel: **Anxious** for Hana and for us, not for **my knife**.
S1.quote: My fish section is fine, but my fiancée Hana answers customers at a bank call centre.
fieldNote: Jamal's anxiety here comes from his **fiancée's job**, not his own.
He defends **free markets** in public while privately fearing their effect at home.
He'd turn to **family before government**, true to his views.

steps.text: Take every extra shift Mr Okafor offers at The Anchor
Cut the wedding guest list from 150 to 80
Ask Hana's mum about work for Hana at her bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's frightening. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the companies' right to build what they build, but someone should have thought about families. I'd say it at church, after the service, where people actually talk. I wouldn't go to a protest, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my fiancée Hana loses her job in 2028 and I lose mine a few years later. That's our whole household in one picture. The Anchor's thinking jobs, the booking and the orders, go first, and then by 2031 a robot can fillet as well as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard from the first month: smaller wedding, no honeymoon abroad, no new car. I'd pay down as much of the flat as I can, so the mortgage can't sink us. And I'd keep cooking at The Anchor as long as Mr Okafor keeps the door open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake next to Hana thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work around 2031. Do you think Daniel would buy one for The Anchor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel would, yes, if it's cheaper. He's not a bad man, he'd just do the maths. Mr Okafor would hate it, but he'd be retired by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I've only ever done one thing, and I'm proud of it. Maybe I'd ask at the boatyard, because my uncle works there and it's hands-on, but robots would get there too.

say: I'd say firms can build what they build, but someone should think about **families**.
I'd say it after **church**, not at a protest.
think: Hana's job goes in **2028** and mine a few years later.
That's our **whole household** in one picture.
do: Cut the wedding, skip the **honeymoon abroad** and drop the new car.
Pay down as much of the **flat** as possible.
S2.quote: My fiancée Hana loses her job in 2028 and I lose mine a few years later. That's our whole household in one picture.
fieldNote: Jamal expects **both household incomes** to go, which drives real fear.
His **resistance** shows in having no second skill to fall back on.
He sees Daniel's choice as **business sense**, not villainy.

steps.text: Drop the honeymoon abroad and the new car purchase
Pay down the flat mortgage with all spare money
Keep cooking at The Anchor as long as it stays open
Hold a smaller wedding and delay starting a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you'd see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before: let businesses compete, but keep apprenticeships going for young people. Someone should be teaching trades, even now. I'd say that at church and to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, but I'd be 34 when the robots come. My fiancée Hana would have three years to find something steadier before AGI hits her call centre in 2031. That's the main difference for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding as planned, but put more of the savings into the flat. I'd stay at The Anchor and maybe ask Mr Okafor to teach me the ordering and the money side, in case I ever run a place. I still wouldn't use AI apps myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you and Hana do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for Hana to switch jobs before the call centre goes. Time to pay off more of the flat. Maybe time to have our first child before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the cooks, not Mr Okafor. The big companies racing ahead, maybe, but that's their right. I'd blame governments if they then hand everyone a cheque instead of helping people learn a new trade.

say: I'd say let businesses compete but keep **apprenticeships** going.
I'd say **trades** should be taught to young people now, at church and to my dad.
think: I'd be **34** when robots come, which is a bit more time.
Hana gets **three years** to move before AGI hits her **call centre**.
do: Keep the wedding as planned and put more savings into **the flat**.
Ask Mr Okafor to teach me **ordering and money** at The Anchor.
S3.quote: My fiancée Hana would have three years to find something steadier before AGI hits her call centre in 2031.
fieldNote: Five years lets Jamal keep **family plans** mostly intact.
He'd blame **governments handing out cheques** more than tech firms.
He'd learn the business side from his mentor, but still **avoid AI apps**.

steps.text: Put more of the savings into paying off the flat
Ask Mr Okafor to teach the ordering and accounts side
Help Hana move to a steadier job before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so nobody should be crying about it. I'd say work hard, save, look after your family. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Hana's call centre still goes in 2036, and I'd be cooking till about 2039. By then I'd hope to have paid off the flat and have two kids in school. It's still an end, but it's far enough away that I can plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married on time, have kids, pay off the flat by about 2034. I'd keep learning the business from Mr Okafor, maybe buy into The Anchor if Daniel doesn't want it. I wouldn't change my job now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at the back of my mind. Not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to about 39 before robots reach the fish section. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sits all right. Most cooks don't last on the line past 40 anyway, their knees go. If the robots come at the same time, maybe I'm managing something by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids, if you have them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn something with their hands and something with their heads. My dad told me to get a trade, and he was right for my time. Their time will need both.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so nobody should be **crying** about it.
I'd say **work hard**, save and look after your family.
think: I'd be cooking till about **2039**, with the flat paid off.
Hana's **call centre** still goes in 2036, but we can plan.
do: Pay off the **flat** by about 2034, while Hana and I start a family.
Learn the business and maybe **buy into The Anchor**.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of my mind, **not scared**.
S4.quote: My dad told me to get a trade, and he was right for my time.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets Jamal follow his **traditional life plan**.
He thinks of **buying into** his mentor's restaurant as a real option.
He still wouldn't change his own work, consistent with his **resistance**.

steps.text: Pay off the flat by about 2034
Keep the fish section at The Anchor and learn the business
Offer to buy a share of The Anchor if Daniel doesn't want it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hana and I would both lose our jobs just as we're starting a family. What would help is real apprenticeships for grown-ups, paid, where you learn a new trade next to someone who knows it. Not a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. I learned to fillet a fish standing next to Mr Okafor for three years. A robot that learns filleting in a week makes my three years beside my old boss Mr Okafor look like nothing. That hurts more than the money.

headlineQuote: A robot that learns filleting in a week makes my three years beside my old boss Mr Okafor look like nothing.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old fish cook** at a harbour seafood restaurant where he trained as an apprentice.
He owns a **part-paid flat**, has strong savings and is marrying Hana, a bank **call centre** worker.
He's **traditional** and avoids technology, trusting trade, family and church.
His mood follows **Hana's job** as much as his own, peaking at **alarmed** in the fastest picture.
He wants **paid adult apprenticeships**, not handouts, if work disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Hana lose their jobs as they start a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for adults, learning a new trade beside someone skilled.
